summaries.example: Imagine describing a line of numbered stepping-stones. First-order logic can say, “Every stone has a number” or “There is a stone after this one.” Second-order logic can also talk about a whole group of stones at once. It can say that a group contains the first stone and contains the next stone whenever it contains one. If every group with those two features contains every stone, the stones behave like the natural numbers.
summaries.summary: Second-order logic is an expanded form of first-order logic. First-order logic can say things about individual objects, such as numbers, and about relations between them. Second-order logic adds variables for properties, relations, and functions. This makes it possible to state ideas such as mathematical induction: a property that holds at zero and continues from one number to the next holds for every natural number. In this way, second-order logic can characterize structures such as the natural numbers and the real numbers more exactly than first-order logic. A theory is categorical when all its models have the same structure, apart from changes in names. However, this power brings difficulties. To explain what it means to quantify over every property, we usually use set theory in the background. Different choices about that background can affect what counts as true. Full second-order logic therefore does not have the same Completeness, Compactness, and model-size results as first-order logic. Henkin, or general, models allow only a selected collection of properties and functions. Under that interpretation, second-order logic has a smoother theory and many first-order-like results. The entry also explains higher-order logic, which can talk about properties of properties, and describes uses in mathematics and computer science.
key_ideas: First-order logic talks about objects. Second-order logic can also quantify over properties and relations.
This extra ability lets second-order logic describe the natural numbers and the real numbers more exactly than first-order logic can.
Second-order logic is stronger than first-order logic in what it can express, but set theory can build longer layers of sets and is stronger in another sense.
The meaning of “all properties” depends on background set theory, so philosophers disagree about how foundational second-order logic is.
With full semantics, important first-order results such as the Completeness and Compactness Theorems do not work in their usual form.
With general or Henkin models, second-order logic behaves more like first-order logic and regains results such as Completeness and Compactness.
summaries.why_it_matters: Second-order logic helps explain how mathematicians describe important structures, including numbers, real numbers, graphs, and trees. It also appears in computer science, especially when studying finite structures and questions about computation. Learning about it shows that adding expressive power to a language can create new problems about meaning, proof, and the background assumptions needed to interpret the language.

important_terms.definition: A formal language for making exact statements about objects, their properties, and their relationships.
A kind of logic that can talk about all the objects in a domain, such as all the numbers being studied.
A kind of logic that can also talk about properties, relations, and functions of objects.
A collection of things being discussed, such as the natural numbers in a number problem.
A rule that assigns each input, or group of inputs, exactly one output.
A sentence or group of sentences that describes a mathematical structure in exactly one way, up to a matching relabeling.

questions_to_think_about: Why might it help to talk about a whole property, such as “being an even number,” instead of only individual numbers?
Is a logic more useful when it describes one structure exactly, or when it has many different models to study?
Why might mathematicians use second-order logic as a tool even if they disagree about its foundations?

summaries.example: Consider the natural numbers with zero and a successor operation. In second-order logic one can state that zero has the relevant starting properties, every number has a successor, successors are distinct in the expected way, and every property containing zero and closed under successor contains every number. This induction condition can characterize the natural-number structure up to isomorphism. First-order logic cannot impose the same characterization: compactness permits nonstandard models containing elements beyond every finite successor sequence.
summaries.summary: Second-order logic extends first-order logic by adding quantification over properties, relations, and functions. In a language for arithmetic, first-order variables range over numbers, while second-order variables can range over sets of numbers or relations among numbers. This permits a single induction principle: any property containing zero and preserved by successor contains every natural number. Together with suitable axioms, that principle characterizes the natural numbers up to isomorphism. Similar second-order descriptions characterize the ordered field of real numbers. These results explain why second-order logic is often called stronger than first-order logic. Yet the comparison with set theory is more complicated. Second-order semantics is normally explained using set theory, and the quantifiers range over subsets and functions of one fixed domain. Set theory, by contrast, can iterate the power-set operation and quantify across a broader hierarchy of domains. Thus second-order logic can be stronger in expressive ability over a structure while weaker as a universal foundation. Full second-order semantics also lacks the ordinary first-order Completeness, Compactness, and Löwenheim–Skolem theorems. Henkin’s general semantics restricts second-order variables to selected collections of relations and functions. It can be treated as a many-sorted first-order framework and supports completeness and compactness, although it no longer has the same full-model categoricity. The entry further examines quantifier hierarchies, non-absoluteness, higher-order logic, type theory, foundations of mathematics, second-order arithmetic, and finite model theory.
key_ideas: The expressive strength of second-order logic comes from quantifying over properties, relations, and functions, not merely individuals.
Full second-order semantics can characterize the natural numbers and the ordered real field up to isomorphism, something first-order logic cannot do.

The comparison with set theory is not one-dimensional: second-order logic is more expressive than first-order logic in some respects, while set theory supports repeated power-set constructions and a more universal range of domains.
Full semantics is non-absolute: whether a second-order sentence is true can depend on the surrounding set-theoretic universe.
The usual first-order Completeness, Compactness, and Löwenheim–Skolem results fail for full semantics, while Henkin semantics restores analogous results.
In finite model theory, existential second-order logic is closely connected with nondeterministic polynomial time, and monadic fragments have important decidability results.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject connects philosophical questions about mathematical existence and truth with technical questions about syntax, semantics, models, and proof. It clarifies why a more expressive language may have weaker proof-theoretic behavior, and why the interpretation of “all properties” cannot be separated from assumptions about sets. Its finite-model applications also link logic with databases, automata, computational complexity, and the study of whether problems can be efficiently recognized.

important_terms.definition: A formal system whose individual variables range over objects and whose quantifiers do not directly range over properties or relations.
A formal system with variables and quantifiers for individuals plus variables and quantifiers for properties, relations, and functions.
The interpretation that second-order variables range over every relevant subset, relation, or function on the domain.
A background language or theory used to define and study the meaning and truth of another formal language.
A theory is categorical when any two of its models are isomorphic; they have the same structure up to relabeling.
A model in which second-order variables range over a chosen collection of relations and functions rather than all of them.
A general model satisfying the comprehension and choice principles used in the relevant deductive system.
The claim that every semantically valid statement can be obtained by a formal proof within an appropriate proof system.

questions_to_think_about: Does the ability to characterize the natural numbers exactly make second-order logic a better foundation for mathematics, or does its dependence on set theory weaken that claim?
Why might the failure of Compactness be viewed as a loss of a useful theorem rather than simply as a defect?
What is gained and what is lost when full semantics is replaced by Henkin semantics?
If second-order logic can express more properties, why does it not automatically provide a complete and effective proof system?

summaries.example: Suppose you are checking whether a number line really has every natural number and no extras. First-order logic can name numbers and describe the next-number rule, but it cannot rule out a strange model with additional elements beyond all the named steps. Second-order logic can talk about every possible group of points. If every group that starts at zero and keeps the next point whenever it has one must include the whole line, the structure is forced to behave like the ordinary natural numbers.
summaries.summary: Second-order logic is a richer version of first-order logic. First-order logic can quantify over individual objects, while second-order logic also quantifies over properties, relations, and functions. For example, when discussing natural numbers, second-order logic can express induction by saying that every property true of zero and preserved by the successor operation is true of every number. This gives second-order descriptions of the natural numbers and, with suitable order and field axioms, the real numbers. Such descriptions are categorical: they determine a structure up to isomorphism, meaning that different models have the same shape even if their elements have different names. First-order logic cannot do this in the same way because results such as Compactness and the Löwenheim–Skolem theorems allow unexpected models. The extra power of second-order logic creates a philosophical problem. Under full semantics, “all properties” is usually understood through set theory. Set theory can also build successive levels of sets, so it is more universal in one sense. This is why second-order logic may be more powerful than first-order logic but less powerful than set theory in another sense. Full semantics is also sensitive to the surrounding set theory and does not have the ordinary first-order Completeness Theorem. Henkin models restrict the available properties and functions; they restore completeness and compactness but change what categoricity means. The entry also discusses higher-order logic, type theory, mathematical foundations, and finite model theory.
key_ideas: Second-order logic adds quantifiers for properties and relations, so it can describe patterns that first-order logic cannot capture.
This extra expressive power can make a theory categorical, as with standard descriptions of the natural numbers and real numbers.
There is a debate about whether second-order logic is a foundation of mathematics or a language whose meaning still depends on set theory.
Full second-order logic does not keep all of first-order logic’s most important model-theoretic theorems.
Henkin models provide a different interpretation in which second-order logic resembles a many-sorted version of first-order logic.
Higher-order logic continues the same idea by allowing talk about properties of properties, while type theory organizes these levels through types.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic shows that mathematical language is not just about writing more symbols. Changing what variables may range over changes what can be expressed, what counts as a model, and which proof theorems remain available. Second-order logic is therefore important both to philosophers asking how mathematics is grounded and to logicians and computer scientists studying structures, algorithms, automata, and complexity.

important_terms.definition: A system for making precise statements about objects and how they are related.
Logic whose variables usually stand for individual objects, such as particular numbers or people.
Logic that can also quantify over properties, groups, relations, and functions involving objects.
The objects, properties, and relationships that a logical language is being used to discuss.
A way of interpreting the symbols of a language in a particular structure.
A description that allows only one structure, apart from renaming its elements.
A model where property and relation variables range over a selected collection, not necessarily every possible one.

questions_to_think_about: Why is talking about every property more powerful than talking only about every object?
Would you prefer a theory that describes one intended structure exactly, or one that has many models that can be compared?
Why might the background theory used to interpret a logic affect the logic’s claims about truth?
How could a logic used for infinite mathematics also be useful for computer science, where finite structures are common?
